CHAPTER XC

It was the day after that terrible scene: the little house in the
Hoog Straet was like a grave, and none more listless and dejected than
Catherine, so busy and sprightly by nature, After dinner, her eyes red
with weeping, she went to the convent to try and soften Gerard, and lay
the first stone at least of a reconciliation.

It was some time before she could make the porter understand whom she
was seeking. Eventually she learned he had left late last night, and was
not expected back, She went sighing with the news to Margaret. She found
her sitting idle, like one with whom life had lost its savour; she had
her boy clasped so tight in her arms, as if he was all she had left, and
she feared some one would take him too. Catherine begged her to come to
the Hoog Straet.

“What for?” sighed Margaret. “You cannot but say to yourselves, she is
the cause of all.”

“Nay, nay,” said Catherine, “we are not so ill-hearted, and Eli is so
fond on you; you will maybe soften him.”

“Oh, if you think I can do any good, I'll come,” said Margaret, with a
weary sigh.

They found Eli and a carpenter putting up another name in place of
Cornelis and Sybrandt's; and what should that name be but Margaret
Brandt's.

With all her affection for Margaret, this went through poor Catherine
like a knife. “The bane of one is another's meat,” said she.

“Can he make me spend the money unjustly?” replied Margaret coldly.

“You are a good soul,” said Catherine. “Ay, so best, sith he is the
strongest.”

The next day Giles dropped in, and Catherine told the story all in
favour of the black sheep, and invited his pity for them, anathematized
by their brother, and turned on the wide world by their father. But
Giles's prejudices ran the other way; he heard her out, and told her
bluntly the knaves had got off cheap; they deserved to be hanged at
Margaret's door into the bargain, and dismissing them with contempt,
crowed with delight at the return of his favourite. “I'll show him,”
 said he, “what 'tis to have a brother at court with a heart to serve a
friend, and a head to point the way.”

“Bless thee, Giles,” murmured Margaret softly.

“Thou wast ever his stanch friend, dear Giles,” said little Kate; “but
alack, I know not what thou canst do for him now.”

Giles had left them, and all was sad and silent again, when a
well-dressed man opened the door softly, and asked was Margaret Brandt
here.

“D'ye hear, lass? You are wanted,” said Catherine briskly. In her the
Gossip was indestructible.

“Well, mother,” said Margaret listlessly, “and here I am.”

A shuffling of feet was heard at the door, and a colourless, feeble old
man was assisted into the room. It was Ghysbrecht Van Swieten. At
sight of him Catherine shrieked, and threw her apron over her head, and
Margaret shuddered violently, and turned her head swiftly away, not to
see him.

A feeble voice issued from the strange visitor's lips, “Good people, a
dying man hath come to ask your forgiveness.”

“Come to look on your work, you mean,” said Catherine, taking down her
apron and bursting out sobbing. “There, there, she is fainting; look to
her, Eli, quick.”

“Nay,” said Margaret, in a feeble voice, “the sight of him gave me a
turn, that is all, Prithee, let him say his say, and go; for he is the
murderer of me and mine.”

“Alas,” said Ghysbrecht, “I am too feeble to say it standing and no one
biddeth me sit down.”

Eli, who had followed him into the house, interfered here, and said,
half sullenly, half apologetically, “Well, burgomaster, 'tis not our
wont to leave a visitor standing whiles we sit. But man, man, you have
wrought us too much ill.” And the honest fellow's voice began to shake
with anger he fought hard to contain, because it was his own house.

Then Ghysbrecht found an advocate in one who seldom spoke in vain in
that family.

It was little Kate. “Father, mother,” said she, “my duty to you, but
this is not well. Death squares all accounts, And see you not death in
his face? I shall not live long, good friends; and his time is shorter
than mine.”

Eli made haste and set a chair for their dying enemy with his own hands.
Ghysbrecht's attendants put him into it. “Go fetch the boxes,” said he.
They brought in two boxes, and then retired, leaving their master alone
in the family he had so cruelly injured.

Every eye was now bent on him, except Margaret's. He undid the boxes
with unsteady fingers, and brought out of one the title-deeds of a
property at Tergou. “This land and these houses belonged to Floris
Brandt, and do belong to thee of right, his granddaughter. These I did
usurp for a debt long since defrayed with interest. These I now restore
their rightful owner with penitent tears. In this other box are three
hundred and forty golden angels, being the rent and fines I have
received from that land more than Floris Brandt's debt to me, I have
kept it compt, still meaning to be just one day; but Avarice withheld
me, pray, good people, against temptation! I was not born dishonest: yet
you see.”

“Well, to be sure!” cried Catherine. “And you the burgomaster! Hast
whipt good store of thieves in thy day. However,” said she, on second
thoughts, “'tis better late than never, What, Margaret, art deaf? The
good man hath brought thee back thine own. Art a rich woman. Alack, what
a mountain o' gold!”

“Bid him keep land and gold, and give me back my Gerard, that he stole
from me with his treason,” said Margaret, with her head still averted.

“Alas!” said Ghysbrecht, “would I could, what I can I have done. Is it
nought? It cost me a sore struggle; and I rose from my last bed to do it
myself, lest some mischance should come between her and her rights.”

“Old man,” said Margaret, “since thou, whose idol is pelf, hast done
this, God and the saints will, as I hope, forgive thee. As for me, I am
neither saint nor angel, but only a poor woman, whose heart thou hast
broken, Speak to him, Kate, for I am like the dead.”

Kate meditated a little while; and then her soft silvery voice fell
like a soothing melody upon the air, “My poor sister hath a sorrow that
riches cannot heal, Give her time, Ghysbrecht; 'tis not in nature she
should forgive thee all. Her boy is fatherless; and she is neither maid,
wife, nor widow; and the blow fell but two days syne, that laid her
heart a bleeding.”

A single heavy sob from Margaret was the comment to these words.

“Therefore, give her time! And ere thou diest, she will forgive thee
all, ay, even to pleasure me, that haply shall not be long behind thee,
Ghysbrecht. Meantime, we, whose wounds be sore, but not so deep as hers,
do pardon thee, a penitent and a dying man; and I, for one, will pray
for thee from this hour; go in peace!”

Their little oracle had spoken; it was enough. Eli even invited him
to break a manchet and drink a stoup of wine to give him heart for his
journey.

But Ghysbrecht declined, and said what he had done was a cordial to him,
“Man seeth but a little way before him, neighbour. This land I clung
so to it was a bed of nettles to me all the time. 'Tis gone; and I feel
happier and livelier like for the loss on't.”

He called his men, and they lifted him into the litter.

When he was gone Catherine gloated over the money. She had never seen
so much together, and was almost angry with Margaret, for “sitting out
there like an image.” And she dilated on the advantages of money.

And she teased Margaret till at last she prevailed on her to come and
look at it.

“Better let her be, mother,” said Kate, “How can she relish gold, with a
heart in her bosom liker lead?” But Catherine persisted.

The result was, Margaret looked down at all her wealth with wondering
eyes. Then suddenly wrung her hands and cried with piercing anguish,
“TOO LATE! TOO LATE!” And shook off her leaden despondency, only to go
into strong hysterics over the wealth that came too late to be shared
with him she loved.

A little of this gold, a portion of this land, a year or two ago, when
it was as much her own as now; and Gerard would have never left her side
for Italy or any other place.

“Too late! Too late!”
generated_text:
The day after the terrible scene, the little house on the Hoog Straet lay heavy with silence, like a tomb. Catherine, usually so brisk and full of life, moved through it as though her spirit had been drained away. Her eyes were red from weeping when, after dinner, she set out for the convent, hoping to find Gerard and begin the slow work of mending what had been broken. She meant to soften his heart, if only by a single word.

It took some time before the porter could understand whom she sought. When he finally did, he told her that Gerard had left late the previous night and was not expected back. Disheartened, Catherine returned home and broke the news to Margaret.

She found her sitting still, motionless, as if all joy had fled from the world. The child clutched tightly in her arms seemed to be all that remained—her last anchor. She held him close, afraid someone might take even this small comfort from her.

“Come to the Hoog Straet,” Catherine urged gently.

“For what?” Margaret whispered, her voice thin and weary. “You must think I am the cause of all this sorrow.”

“No, no,” Catherine said quickly. “We are not so cruel. And Eli loves you—he may yet be won over.”

“If I can help,” Margaret murmured, “then I will go.”

They arrived to find Eli and a carpenter replacing the old sign—once bearing the names Cornelis and Sybrandt—with a new one: *Margaret Brandt*. Catherine’s heart sank. Though she loved Margaret deeply, this act pierced her like a knife.

“The bane of one is another’s meat,” she muttered.

“You cannot make me spend money unjustly,” Margaret replied coldly.

“You are a good soul,” Catherine said, trying to keep her voice steady.

“Aye,” Margaret answered, “but best, since he is the strongest.”

The next day, Giles dropped in. Catherine told him the tale, painting the brothers as victims—outcast by their father, abandoned by their kin. She pleaded for pity, for justice, for mercy.

But Giles saw things differently. He listened patiently, then spoke plainly: “Those rogues got off too lightly. They deserve to hang at Margaret’s door. And now—hurrah!—my favourite returns.” He smiled broadly, his pride restored. “I’ll show him,” he declared, “what it means to have a brother at court who knows how to serve a friend and guide him right.”

“Bless you, Giles,” Margaret whispered softly.

“You’ve always stood by him, dear Giles,” little Kate added. “But alas, I know not what you can do now.”

Giles left, and silence settled once more—until a quiet knock at the door.

A well-dressed man stepped inside, asking if Margaret Brandt was there.

“Hear this, lass!” Catherine called cheerfully. “You’re wanted!”

“Well, mother,” Margaret said dully, “here I am.”

Then came the shuffle of feet. A frail, pale old man was helped into the room—Ghysbrecht Van Swieten.

At the sight of him, Catherine gasped and threw her apron over her face. Margaret shuddered violently, turning her head sharply away, refusing to look.

A weak voice trembled from the visitor’s lips: “Good people, a dying man has come to beg your forgiveness.”

“Come to see the ruin you made,” Catherine snapped, pulling down her apron and breaking into sobs.

“There, there—she faints! Eli, quick, help her!”

“No,” Margaret said faintly. “It’s just the shock. Let him speak. But he is the murderer of me and mine.”

“Alas,” Ghysbrecht whispered, “I am too weak to stand. No one offers me a seat.”

Eli, who had followed him in, stepped forward, half angry, half ashamed. “Well, burgomaster,” he said stiffly, “it is not our custom to leave guests standing while we sit. But mark this—your actions have done us great harm.”

His voice shook, but he held himself in check—for this was his own home.

Then, unexpectedly, a soft voice broke the tension.

“Father, mother,” little Kate said gently, “I owe you my duty—but this is not right. Death settles all accounts. See how death stares from his face? I shall not live long. His time is shorter than mine.”

Eli hesitated, then hurried to bring a chair. With careful hands, he placed it before the dying man. Ghysbrecht’s attendants helped him sit.

“Fetch the boxes,” he said.

They brought two wooden chests and withdrew, leaving the old man alone among those he had wronged.

All eyes turned to him—except Margaret’s.

With trembling fingers, Ghysbrecht opened the first box and pulled out deeds. “This land and these houses belonged to Floris Brandt,” he said. “They belong to you, his granddaughter, by right. I took them once, for a debt long paid with interest. Now I return them—tears in my heart, and shame in my soul.”

He opened the second box. “Three hundred forty golden angels—the rent and fines I collected beyond what was owed. I kept them… thinking I would give them back one day. But greed held me fast. I was not born dishonest—but I became so. Forgive me, please, against temptation.”

“Indeed!” Catherine exclaimed. “And you, burgomaster—the man who punished thieves all your life! But better late than never. Margaret, can you hear? He’s given you back your own. You’re rich now. Alack, what a mountain of gold!”

“Let him keep land and gold,” Margaret said, her head still turned away. “Give me back my Gerard—the one you stole from me with your treachery.”

“Alas,” Ghysbrecht said, “I wish I could. But what I can do, I have done. It cost me much. I rose from my deathbed to do it myself, lest misfortune prevent you from claiming what is yours.”

“Old man,” Margaret said quietly, “you, whose god is gold, have done this. God and the saints may forgive you, I hope. As for me—I am no saint. I am only a woman, broken-hearted. Speak to him, Kate. I am already dead.”

Kate paused, then spoke in a voice like music, gentle and clear: “My sister carries a grief no riches can heal. Give her time, Ghysbrecht. It is not natural she should forgive you all at once. Her son is fatherless. She is neither maid nor wife nor widow. The blow fell only two days ago—and it laid her heart open, bleeding.”

A deep, silent sob escaped Margaret.

“Therefore, give her time,” Kate continued. “And before you die, she may forgive you—even to please me, who may soon follow you, Ghysbrecht. In the meantime, we—whose wounds are deep, but not as deep as hers—forgive you. You are penitent, and dying. And I, for one, will pray for you from this hour. Go in peace.”

Her words fell like a blessing. Even Eli offered the old man bread and wine, but Ghysbrecht declined.

“What I have done,” he said, “is enough to strengthen me. Man sees only a little way ahead. That land I clung to so tightly—it was a bed of nettles all along. Now it is gone—and I feel lighter, freer, as though I have shed a burden.”

He called for his men. They lifted him into a litter and carried him away.

When he was gone, Catherine lingered over the gold, dazzled by its weight and glow. She had never seen such wealth gathered in one place. She nearly scolded Margaret for staying behind like a statue.

“Oh, come and see!” she insisted, teasing her. “Think of the possibilities!”

“Leave her be, mother,” Kate said softly. “How can she enjoy gold when her heart is heavier than lead?”

But Catherine pressed on. At last, Margaret relented.

She stood before the treasure, staring, wide-eyed. Then suddenly, she wrung her hands and screamed: “TOO LATE! TOO LATE!”

She collapsed into sobs, overwhelmed—not by riches, but by the agony of what might have been. If only a fraction of this wealth, a piece of this land, had come to her a year or two ago—when it was truly hers—Gerard would never have left. He would never have gone to Italy, never have chosen another path.

“Too late! Too late!” she cried again, her voice breaking with sorrow.
